title: Area II review: Technical Subject Areas
intro: These questions mix the four Tasks of Area II: flight instruments and navigation equipment, aeromedical factors, IFR regulations and publications, and logbook entries for instrument instruction. Most join two of them in one instructing situation, such as an instrument failure that turns into a rule or reporting question, an aeromedical problem before an IPC or on an approach, or a lesson that ends with the entry you write in the logbook.

questions.q: Runup before an IFR lesson in your school's six-pack trainer, where one vacuum pump drives the attitude and heading indicators: the electric turn coordinator's miniature airplane does not move in taxi turns. Your learner says the attitude indicator shows bank anyway, so the flight can go. What do you teach?
options: No IFR today: 91.205(d) requires a gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator here, and it backs up bank if the vacuum fails
It can go: 91.205(d) asks only for a slip-skid indicator, and the ball in the turn coordinator still works fine
It can go in daylight: a rate-of-turn indicator is on the 91.205 list only for IFR flight at night
It can go: her attitude indicator is the third attitude system that 91.205(d)(3) accepts in its place
questions.why: For IFR, 91.205(d) requires a gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator, except in an airplane with a third attitude instrument system usable through 360 degrees of pitch and roll, and it lists the slip-skid indicator as a separate item [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. A trainer whose only attitude indicator runs on its one vacuum pump has no third system, so the tempting 'ball still works' answer covers only one of the two items. The turn coordinator is also the backup source of bank information if the attitude indicator fails, which is why most airplanes power the gyros from at least two sources [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. The night items are a separate list that IFR adds to; nothing limits the rate-of-turn requirement to night [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

questions.q: On your learner's last IFR lesson, water froze in the static line and she flew home on the alternate static source. Today a mechanic disconnected a static line, drained it and reconnected it. The 24-month altimeter and static test was done in March. What is needed before your next IFR flight in controlled airspace?
options: Nothing more: the March test stays valid for 24 calendar months, whatever is done to the static lines
A new static system test and inspection, since the system has been opened and closed since March
A new test because she used the alternate static source in flight, which counts as opening the system
Only a VOR check, since 91.411 covers the altimeter instrument itself but not the static lines
questions.why: 91.411(a)(1) asks for tests of each static pressure system, altimeter and altitude reporting system within the preceding 24 calendar months, and 91.411(a)(2) adds that, except for the use of system drain and alternate static pressure valves, any opening and closing of the static pressure system must be followed by a test and inspection before IFR flight in controlled airspace [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]]. So the March test does not cover the reconnected line, while her in-flight use of the alternate static valve needed no new test by itself. The alternate source is there for this case: it supplies static pressure if the primary source is blocked, with the altimeter reading slightly high and the airspeed high [[23:98|IFH 5-3]], and moisture, including ice, is a common cause of a blockage [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].

questions.q: In cloud, your learner's PFD suddenly looks like this. The airplane matches the IFH example: standby attitude indicator, airspeed indicator, altimeter and compass, an autopilot, and no standby turn coordinator. She says she feels a right turn and starts to roll left. What do you coach?
options: Keep the ball centered on the PFD's slip-skid indicator, since coordination is what defeats a false turn
Use the compass as her bank reference; the IFH rates it as useful as a turn coordinator in this failure
Use the autopilot's roll and altitude hold to cut workload; fly the standby attitude indicator, not the feeling
Disconnect the autopilot, because an AHRS failure takes away every one of its modes along with the attitude display
questions.why: When the AHRS fails, all attitude and heading indications on the PFD are lost, with the unusual attitude protection, and every autopilot mode except roll and altitude hold is lost. The slip-skid indicator is gone too, and with no standby turn coordinator the compass shows a heading but is not as useful as a turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The IFH says to use the autopilot to reduce workload, which also lowers the chance of an unusual attitude, and the standby attitude indicator remains [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Her feeling of a turn is a sensation to disregard: trust the instruments [[23:76|IFH 3-9]], and never try to recover by sensations other than sight [[23:190|IFH 7-29]].

questions.q: In IMC in a glass-panel trainer, the alternator fails. The destination is 35 minutes away and a suitable airport is 12 minutes away. Your learner says the main battery is good for about 40 minutes, so she wants to press on. What do you teach?
options: Press on but shed load: in a glass airplane the IFH calls an alternator failure an abnormal, not an emergency
Press on and arm the standby battery now, since the IFH says to arm it only after the charging system fails
Press on: the standby battery adds so much time that the 40-minute figure can be treated as a firm minimum
Divert to the nearby airport, shed load and tell ATC: the IFH says never to continue once charging has failed
questions.why: The IFH's 40 minutes of battery is an approximation that should not be relied on, and at no time should a pilot consider continuing a flight once the charging system has failed: land at the nearest suitable airport and reduce the electrical load [[23:330|IFH 11-5]]. In a glass airplane the AHRS, ADC and engine indicating system run on electrical power, so the failure is an emergency, not the abnormal it was in round-dial airplanes; the standby battery comes on only if its switch is in ARM, and arming should be done before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. Advise ATC of the impending electrical failure [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

questions.q: In the knowledge portion of an IPC, a pilot whose six-pack airplane has no vacuum warning light says he does not scan the suction gauge: if the pump quits, the attitude indicator will tumble at once and he will know. How do you handle it?
options: Correct it now: the gyros slow and wander, so the gauge stays in his scan, and it is IPC material
Accept it: a gyro that loses suction tumbles right away, so the attitude indicator is itself the warning
Accept it, since AC 61-98E limits the IPC to ACS flight tasks and leaves aircraft systems to flight reviews
Correct it after the flight: AC 61-98E checks equipment failures in the skill portion, not in the oral part
questions.why: When the vacuum pump fails, the attitude and heading indicators fail progressively: as the gyros slow down they may wander, a pilot who misses the failure can turn a benign situation into a hazardous one, and because many small airplanes have no vacuum failure warning the pilot should monitor the suction gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. AC 61-98E puts this in the IPC knowledge portion: aircraft systems with emergency procedures due to equipment failure, and flight instruments and navigation equipment with emergency procedures for malfunction or failure [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]]. So it is neither outside the IPC nor something to leave until after the flight.

questions.q: Your learner plans a 2-hour night IFR flight at 9,000 feet in an unpressurized airplane with no oxygen aboard. After reading AIM 8-1-2 he says the flight would be illegal without oxygen. What do you teach?
options: Illegal: AIM procedures become binding once a flight is under IFR, so the 5,000-foot night figure applies
Legal: the rule starts above 12,500 feet, but the AIM's night advice is sound for a personal minimum
Illegal: 91.211 has the flight crew use oxygen above 5,000 feet at night, matching the AIM
Legal, and the AIM advice can be set aside, since hypoxia does nothing to a healthy pilot below 12,000 feet
questions.why: 91.211(a) first requires oxygen for the required flight crew at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet up to and including 14,000 feet, for the part of the flight there lasting more than 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. The AIM itself keeps the two apart: for optimum protection pilots are encouraged to use oxygen above 10,000 feet by day and above 5,000 feet at night, while the CFRs require crew oxygen only from the 12,500-foot band up [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Advice in the AIM does not become a rule because the flight is IFR. The tempting 'set it aside' answer is wrong for a night flight: night vision deteriorates at a cabin pressure altitude as low as 5,000 feet, even though other significant effects usually wait until 12,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].

questions.q: Your learner surfaced at 2000 last night from a dive that needed no decompression stops. At 1000 today he wants to fly an IFR trip in his pressurized single; one airway segment has a 9,000-foot MEA and no MOCA. What do you tell him?
options: Go: 12 hours have passed since a no-decompression dive, and the AIM's wait times do not change with altitude
Go, but file 8,000 feet on that segment so that he stays under the altitude where the 24-hour wait applies
Wait: above 8,000 feet MSL the AIM wants 24 hours after any dive, and 91.177 keeps him at or above that MEA
Go: the AIM's wait times count cabin altitude, and his pressurized cabin will stay well below 8,000 feet
questions.why: The AIM recommends at least 12 hours after a dive that needed no decompression stops before flight altitudes up to 8,000 feet, but at least 24 hours after any dive before flight altitudes above 8,000 feet, and these are actual flight altitudes MSL, not pressurized cabin altitudes, to allow for a decompression in flight [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. Under IFR he may not fly below the part 95 MEA, and going down to a MOCA needs a published MOCA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]; the IFR en route low altitude chart is where he finds both [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]]. So 8,000 feet on that segment is not an option, and 14 hours is short of 24.

questions.q: Your learner drifts into a building cell in cloud with the autopilot in altitude hold. A strong updraft hits; she says it feels like a steep climb and reaches to push the nose down. What do you teach?
options: Leave altitude hold engaged: the autopilot is not fooled by illusions, so it holds altitude better than she can
Push to hold the assigned altitude exactly, since ATC expects it and the autopilot alone cannot keep up
Reduce power to idle to stop the climb, hold altitude with pitch, then turn back out the way she came in
Disengage altitude hold, hold a level attitude and let altitude vary; the climb she feels is the elevator illusion
questions.why: An abrupt upward vertical acceleration, as in an updraft, can stimulate the otolith organs to create the illusion of being in a climb, and the disoriented pilot may push the airplane into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. In a thunderstorm the AIM and the IFH say to disengage the autopilot's altitude hold and speed hold, because they increase maneuvering and structural stress, and to keep a constant attitude while altitude and airspeed fluctuate [[34:121|AIM 7-1-27]] [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]. The AIM also says not to change power settings and not to turn back once inside the storm [[34:121|AIM 7-1-27]].

questions.q: You gave no instruction yesterday. Since 0800 today you have given 2.0 hours of ground training, 5.5 hours of flight training in the airplane and a 1.5-hour AATD lesson. At 1900 a learner asks for a 2.0-hour night IFR lesson with approaches. What applies?
options: Legal: only flight training in an aircraft counts, so 7.5 hours; then run IMSAFE on yourself
Not legal: the AATD lesson counts as flight training under 61.195(a), so the day would reach 9.0 hours
Legal under 61.195(a), and with the 8-hour cap built in, fatigue does not need to enter the decision
Not legal: 61.195(a) counts every hour of instruction, ground and device included, so you would reach 11.0
questions.why: 61.195(a) bars a flight instructor from conducting more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]], and part 61 defines flight training as training, other than ground training, received from an authorized instructor in flight in an aircraft [[60:186|14 CFR 61.1(b)]]. The ground and AATD hours do not count, so the day would total 7.5. The rule is a ceiling, not a fitness check: the aeromedical risks of instruction require you to watch your own state as well as the learner's [[25:190|AIH 10-6]], monitored with the IMSAFE model [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and the AIH warns that late night and fatigue lower a pilot's guard just as a night instrument approach in weather comes up [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

questions.q: Cleared to descend from 7,000 to 3,000 feet on an IFR arrival, your learner, who has a mild cold, gets sharp pain above her eyebrows that worsens as she descends. What do you do?
options: Level off now and tell ATC later: 91.123 lets a pilot deviate whenever a crewmember is in pain
Ask ATC for a slower descent, since a slow rate can ease the pain; report if unable to keep 500 fpm
Keep the normal rate: a sinus block happens mostly in the climb, so the pain eases as the pressure rises
Have her use her decongestant spray now, since the AIM says sprays protect adequately against a block
questions.why: A sinus block occurs most often during descent, and slow descent rates can reduce the pain [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]. The AIM says decongestant sprays and drops usually do not give adequate protection, that the block is prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection, and that a block which does not clear shortly after landing calls for a physician [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. Under a clearance the pilot may not deviate without an amended clearance unless an emergency exists or for a TCAS resolution advisory [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]], and the AIM asks for a report whenever the airplane is unable to climb or descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

questions.q: On November 3, 2026, a pilot shows you his logbook. His last six approaches, holding and course tracking were flown under the hood with a safety pilot in April 2026, and nothing since. He asks whether he now needs an IPC. What do you tell him?
options: Yes: once the six-month window has closed for any reason, an IPC is the only way back to IFR currency
No: he is still current through November, as April is within six calendar months of now
No: he lapsed only this month, so logging the 61.57(c) tasks, such as with a safety pilot, restores it
No, but after a lapse the tasks count only in an aircraft, since device time is accepted only in an IPC
questions.why: To act as PIC under IFR he needs six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. For a November flight that window is May through October, so April no longer counts, though it did for October flights. Only a pilot who has failed to meet 61.57(c) for more than six calendar months must take an IPC [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]; the IFH puts it as another 6 months to meet the minimums [[23:11|IFH viii]]. The tasks may be done in an aircraft or in an FFS, FTD or ATD that represents the category [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]], and he logs each approach's location and type and the safety pilot's name [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].

questions.q: Inside the final approach fix on an ILS in IMC, your learner's glideslope flag appears and stays; the localizer needle is steady. The chart also publishes LOC minimums. What do you teach her to do?
options: Go missed at once: when either ILS component fails, neither the ILS nor the localizer approach is authorized
Continue to the ILS decision altitude on the localizer alone, because the approach was briefed as an ILS
Continue to the decision altitude and report it after landing, as 91.187 covers only failures before the FAF
Fly it as the localizer approach, to its MDA and missed approach point, and report the loss to ATC when practical
questions.why: When the localizer fails, an ILS approach is not authorized, but when the glide slope fails the ILS reverts to a non-precision localizer approach [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9]], so the DA no longer applies and the LOC MDA and missed approach point do. In controlled airspace under IFR the PIC must report in-flight malfunctions of navigation, approach or communication equipment to ATC as soon as practical, with the aircraft identification, equipment affected, degree of impairment and assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]; the AIM lists partial loss of ILS receiver capability among these reports [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]. Application: on every ILS, brief the LOC minimums and how the missed approach point is identified, so this switch is easy.

questions.q: Tomorrow night your learner flies an approach to an unfamiliar airport whose runway slopes uphill, and the last part will be visual. Where should she look for runway slope and lighting, and what will the slope tend to make her do?
options: The Chart Supplement and airport diagram; the upslope makes her feel high, so she tends to fly low
The IFR en route low chart's airport data; the upslope will make her feel low, so she will tend to fly high
The AIM's airport listings in Chapter 9; the upslope will make her feel high, so she will tend to fly low
The Chart Supplement and the airport diagram; the upslope will make her feel low, so she will tend to fly high
questions.why: The PHAK says to anticipate visual illusions at unfamiliar airports, especially at night or in bad weather, and to consult airport diagrams and the Chart Supplement U.S. (formerly the A/FD) for runway slope, terrain and lighting; keep the altimeter in the scan and use an electronic glideslope, VASI or PAPI when available [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]]. An upsloping runway creates the illusion that the airplane is higher than it is, so the pilot who does not recognize it flies a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. The Chart Supplement holds data that cannot readily be charted, such as lighting codes [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]]; Chapter 9 of the AIM describes that publication rather than listing airports itself.

questions.q: ATC assigns your learner an RNAV STAR. His IFR GPS database is current but does not contain that STAR. He has the chart and offers to build the arrival waypoint by waypoint from it. What do you teach?
options: Build it: holding the approved chart is all the AIM requires for any STAR, RNAV or not
Decline it with ATC: RNAV STARs must be retrievable by name from the database; accepting is his call
Accept it and expect vectors, since a STAR's routing is only planning data, like its expect altitudes
Build it, then check each waypoint against the chart, since a hand-built arrival is legal once verified
questions.why: Using any STAR requires at least the approved chart, and RNAV STARs must also be retrievable by procedure name from the aircraft database and conform to the charted procedure; accepting or refusing an issued STAR is the pilot's responsibility, and 'NO STAR' in the flight plan remarks tells ATC in advance [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]]. A current database can still lack a procedure, because the avionics manufacturer decides what goes in it [[29:263|IPH 6-13]]. Only the 'expect' altitudes and speeds on a STAR are planning information; a STAR issued by ATC is part of the clearance [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].

questions.q: An IPC candidate has studied IFH page viii, which says the IPC uses tasks from the instrument rating practical test standards. Which standard do you use for his check?
options: The instrument rating PTS, since the IFH is the FAA's current handbook for instrument instructors
The CFII PTS, FAA-S-8081-9E, since an instructor with an instrument rating is the one giving the check
The Instrument Rating ACS areas of operation and Rating Task Table, plus any maneuver you need
Any tasks you choose, since 61.57(d) leaves the content of the check to the instructor who signs it
questions.why: 61.57(d)(1) says the IPC must include the areas of operation of the applicable Airman Certification Standards for the rating held [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]], and AC 61-98E says the maneuvers must include those in the Rating Task Table of the Instrument Rating ACS, with the instructor free to add any others needed [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]]. The airplane ACS that part 61 incorporates is FAA-S-ACS-8C, while FAA-S-8081-9E is the standard for your own CFII test [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(b)(5)]] [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(a)(4)]]. The IFH's PTS wording is out of date [[23:11|IFH viii]], and the IFH says its own wording does not add to or change any 14 CFR duty [[23:6|IFH iii]].

questions.q: Your IPC candidate took a nighttime cold medicine with diphenhydramine at 2200, labeled for a dose every 6 hours. At 0800 he says he feels fine and wants to do the ground review and the flight today. What do you do?
options: Fly it today: the 8-hour rule in 91.17 is about alcohol only, and his dose was taken 10 hours ago
Do the ground review now and sign A.71 today, noting that the flight portion will follow later
Fly it with you as PIC, since the medication rules apply only to a pilot acting as pilot in command
Do the ground review, sign it as ground training given, and fly the check at least 30 hours after the dose
questions.why: The PHAK says to wait at least five maximal dosing intervals after a medication with potentially adverse side effects such as sedation; a 5- to 6-hour interval means 30 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and stays in the system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]], and the safest rule is not to fly as a crewmember while taking any medication unless the FAA approves it [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. 91.17(a) covers drugs that affect the faculties contrary to safety, not only alcohol [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. You must sign the logbook of each person you give ground training [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(a)]], but you may not endorse an IPC until you have tested the pilot under 61.57(d) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]], and A.71 certifies a satisfactorily completed check [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]].

questions.q: A pilot asks you for an IPC in his airplane, which has a glass PFD and MFD and an autopilot you have never used. All your instrument instructing has been in six-pack trainers, though your ratings cover the airplane. What do you do?
options: Decline unless you first get proficient in that make and model, and help him find a qualified instructor
Accept: your ratings cover the category and class, and AC 61-98E asks only that the pilot be proficient
Accept, since glass failure indications are standardized and mirror the six-pack ones you teach well
Accept, and have him explain the avionics as he flies, since the IPC tests his knowledge of them, not yours
questions.why: AC 61-98E says an instructor should be qualified in each specific make and model in which they instruct, should weigh that before accepting an IPC, and if not proficient should honestly decline and help the pilot find a qualified instructor [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4.1]]. The AIH adds that instructors should be familiar with the aircraft, avionics and procedures, since any unfamiliarity creates a hazard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Glass is not a six-pack with screens: failure indications of electronic displays may be entirely different from conventional instruments, and they are not standardized [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

questions.q: After a 1.5-hour lesson, 1.2 of it under the hood with the attitude and heading indicators covered, you write in your learner's logbook: 'Partial panel: compass and timed turns, partial panel VOR approach. Sim inst 1.2. /s/ 11-03-2026 J. J. Jones 987654321CFI.' Compare the sample. What does 61.51(h)(2) still need?
options: Nothing more: a description, the simulated time and a signature with certificate number meet it
The lesson length, 1.5, and your recent experience end date after the certificate number
The location and type of the VOR approach, which 61.51(h) requires in every instrument lesson
Your printed name and the date your instructor certificate was issued, beside the signature
questions.why: 61.51(h)(2) requires training time to be endorsed legibly by the authorized instructor and to include a description of the training, the length of the training lesson, and the instructor's signature, certificate number and certificate expiration date or recent experience end date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]. Here the lesson length (1.5, not just the 1.2 simulated) and the RE date are missing; AC 61-65K shows the format, with the printed name optional [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]]. The location and type of each approach is required by 61.51(g)(3) for approaches used toward 61.57(c) currency, not by 61.51(h) [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]]. Covering the attitude gyro and heading indicator is how partial panel is flown [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and the description should say so.

questions.q: A pilot whose instrument currency lapsed over a year ago wants his IPC tomorrow in actual IMC on an IFR flight plan, with you as PIC. Your own 61.57(c) instrument currency has also lapsed. What do you tell him?
options: We can go: as the authorized instructor giving an IPC, I am exempt from 61.57(c) while I am PIC
We can go with him as PIC, because the IPC flight makes him current from the moment of takeoff
Neither of us may be PIC under IFR, so we fly the check under VFR with a view-limiting device instead
We can go: AC 61-98E only asks me to consider my own instrument currency, so it is advice and not a rule
questions.why: A person may act as PIC under IFR only after meeting the 61.57(c) instrument experience [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]], and 61.57(e) lifts the whole section only for certain part 121 and 135 pilots, while its other exceptions, including the part 125 one and the one for flight training, reach only the takeoff and landing rules of (a) and (b) [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(e)]] [[60:241|14 CFR 61.57(e)(5)]]. He has been lapsed more than six calendar months, so only a completed IPC restores his currency [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. AC 61-98E asks you to consider your own instrument currency before an IPC [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]], advice that sits on top of the rule, not in place of it. The check may be flown under VFR with a view-limiting device, and then you must stay vigilant for other aircraft through every phase [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.1]].

questions.q: In VMC you give your instrument learner the IFH disorientation demonstrations: you fly several while her eyes are closed, then she flies one with eyes closed, following your control instructions. They take 0.4 hours. How is that 0.4 logged?
options: As simulated instrument time for her, since her eyes were closed and she could not see outside at all
Not at all for her: training time counts only while the learner is flying the airplane herself
As instrument time for you, since you were flying the airplane while she could see nothing outside
As training she received, described as disorientation demonstrations, but not as instrument time
questions.why: Instrument time may be logged only for flight time when the person operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, and an instructor logs instrument time only when giving instrument instruction in actual conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]] [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]]. In these demonstrations the learner either is not flying or flies with her eyes closed by your instructions, and they are never flown at low altitude or without an instructor or safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]], so neither of you logs instrument time. It is still training received from an authorized instructor in an aircraft, logged with a description and the length of the lesson [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(h)(1)]] [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]].
